entries.test: The original Sora ant video would show whether its depicted ants have anatomically incorrect leg counts.
entries.note: The anatomical criticism is implicit but clear in context.

entries.test: Representative evidence of children's educational video consumption since publication would show whether plausible but factually incorrect AI videos have become a widespread source of learning for their generation.
entries.note: “A whole generation” has a plain population-level reading, without requiring every child. The imminent horizon can be assessed by the evaluation date.

entries.test: A publicly documented subsequent case of someone mistaking a fake Sora video for authentic footage would establish the prediction.
entries.note: The guarantee is firm and has no explicit deadline.

entries.test: Documented deceptive photorealistic videos made with Sora or open-source counterparts and monetized through advertising shortly after publication would establish the predicted practice.
entries.note: The commercial purpose can be assessed through public monetization records and documented operations. “In short order” is assessable by the evaluation date.

entries.test: Public releases and demonstrated capabilities would show whether open-source counterparts to Sora emerged.
entries.note: He firmly predicts that counterparts will emerge. “In short order” directly modifies scammers' activity, which could use Sora alone, so a deadline for the counterparts is not clearly committed to.

entries.test: Representative studies of ordinary video-platform users distinguishing authentic footage from photorealistic AI fakes would show whether users can reliably identify which is legitimate.
entries.note: The preceding sentence supplies the predicted setting rather than an explicit conditional antecedent. The claim has no separate deadline.
“Likely” explicitly qualifies the predicted damage. YouTube is the educational resource identified in context.
“A wild ride” conveys apprehension without committing to a testable outcome.
